Cuba: Training Third World Guerrillas Over the past 27 years, Cuba's training and support of Third World guerrillas have become institutionalized within its political and govern- mental system. The complex network backing these programs involves party, foreign ministry, military, and intelligence elements. Even Cuba's mass organizations and commercial and cultural entities contribute to the training, equipping, funding, and transporting of leftist groups around the globe. The development of this apparatus into an international operation capable of training hundreds of insurgents per year portends continuing challenges for the United States as it grapples with Havana's efforts to elsewhere. export revolution to the Third World. Despite Cuba's current economic crunch, we see little likelihood that Havana will soon reduce its support to radicals. Moreover, there are increasing signs that Cuba-because of Nicaragua's widening participa- tion in the training of guerrilla forces-may now be able to improve some insurgent groups' chances for success by focusing its resources on providing more specialized training, individually tailored to their needs. Over the longer term, this development could foreshadow stronger insurgent pres- sure on those governments targeted by Cuba in Latin America and leftist groups. he decision to assist a particular guerrilla group ultimately rests with Fidel Castro and the top members of the Cuban Communist Party. Responsibility for implementing the party's "liberation" programs in the Western Hemisphere falls to the Central Committee's America Department (AD), while its General Depart- ment of Foreign Relations (DGRE) handles these duties elsewhere. We believe that both of these organizations are given wide latitude by Castro in coordinating Havana's provision of training, supplies, and funds to radical guerrillas sent to Cuba for training 25X1 25X1 25X1 25X1 probably are turned over to the Ministry of Interior's General Directorate of Special Troops (DGTE)-an elite paramilitary force of some 2,000 personnel. Cuba's guerrilla training 25X1 programs consist of highly specialized and structured courses of instruction in infantry and artillery tactics, explosives, communications, frogman training, concealment techniques and devices, photography, and false documentation. 25X1 Secret ALA 86-10050 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/01/03: CIA-RDP88T00768R000400500001-7 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/01/03: CIA-RDP88T00768R000400500001-7 Secret of at least two major guerrilla training centers in Cuba, and we have located several other facilities that probably function at least periodically in the training of insurgents. In our judgment, most of the groups that we have identified as currently being trained by Cuba can probably be accommodated in these training facilities, which we conserva- tively estimate are handling some 600 to 800 trainees per year. In addition, other, more specialized training-for which we are unable to calculate the number of trainees-almost certainly occurs at other military installations scattered throughout Cuba. Clientele for Cuba's guerrilla training programs include groups from Central and South America as well as Africa and the Middle East. In Central America, the survival of the Sandinista regime in Nicaragua- where Cuba's training efforts are now focused on conventional military programs-remains Havana's highest priority. Guerrilla forces in El Salvador and Guatemala still receive attention from Havana, but the Honduran and Costa Rican radicals have become attractive to the Cubans as they search for ways to reduce pressure on their Nicaraguan ally. Castro also apparently sees new opportuni- ties in southern Africa, where he has shown an uncommon interest in South Africa's mounting domestic problems. As a result, the Cuban leader appears to be gambling that increased Cuban support for terrorist opera- tions in South Africa will aid regional radical groups-and ultimately Havana's major ally in the region, Angola-by causing Pretoria to become preoccupied with internal security. Castro's fervor for promoting armed revolution, long regarded as the core of Cuban Communist philosophy, underscores his willingness to act boldly. In this regard, we see no evidence of a slackening of effort by Havana to carry out its strategy of subversion, although Cuba presumably will remain responsive to outside pressures in its choice of tactics. In the aftermath of the US action in Grenada and Libya, we believe Havana is likely to sidestep requests for support that might be construed as direct Cuban sponsorship of terrorist acts against Americans, lest they elicit such a strong response from Washington that Cuba itself could be threatened. 25X25X1 25X1 25X1 25X1 25X1 25X1 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/01/03: CIA-RDP88T00768R000400500001-7 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/01/03: CIA-RDP88T00768R000400500001-7 Summary Insurgent Training Apparatus Major Guerrilla Training Camps 9 Suspected Training Facilities 13 A. Extract from Article 12 of the Cuban Constitution Since 1959, Cuban President Fidel Castro has viewed the support of Third World revolutionary movements as a vital instrument of Cuba's foreign policy. Re- garded by Castro as a highly effective means of carrying out his "liberation" policies outside normal diplomatic or political channels, Havana's guerrilla training programs have evolved over the years to become an institutionalized part of Cuba's political and governmental infrastructure. Discouraged by the failure of several Cuban-backed insurgencies in Afri- ca and Latin America during the early and middle 1960s, Moscow pressed Havana to shift its support away from regional guerrilla groups to local Commu- nist party affiliates as the primary means of carrying out the revolutionary struggle-a policy that lasted through the mid-1970s. By 1978, however, the Castro regime-encouraged by the success of its expedition- ary forces in Angola and Ethiopia-began to re- appraise its policy regarding the support of groups that advocate armed struggle to seize power. The Sandinista overthrow of the Somoza regime in Nicaragua in July 1979 clearly had a profound effect on Castro's thinking regarding Cuban support of subversion in Latin America, resulting in a return to a more active policy of supporting guerrilla movements in the region, especially in Central America. Castro, apparently confident that events in Nicaragua would lead to revolution throughout Central America, moved to increase Cuba's training and logistic support for the insurgents in El Salvador and Guatemala. The failure of the Salvadoran guerrillas' "final offensive" in January 1981, and active US moves to stem the flow of Cuban arms into the region, however, handed Havana a series of political and military setbacks. These were compounded by US willingness to use military force to protect its interests abroad-as demonstrated in Grenada in October 1983 and against Libya in 1986-as well as by the reemergence of democratic institutions throughout Latin America. Although these events-as with the failures of the 1960s-probably have caused Havana again to re- evaluate its tactics, we believe Castro's longtime strategy for promoting and supporting armed revolu- tion in the Third World remains virtually undis- turbed. Insurgent Training Apparatus Over the past 27 years, the guerrilla training appara- tus in Cuba has matured into a complex network of party, foreign ministry, military, and intelligence elements. Even mass organizations, as well as com- mercial and cultural entities, contribute to the train- ing, equipping, transporting, and funding of leftist and revolutionary groups around the globe. This extensive infrastructure has as its principal long-term goal the systematic destabilization of governments targeted for overthrow by Havana. 25X1 25X1 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/01/03: CIA-RDP88T00768R000400500001-7 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/01/03: CIA-RDP88T00768R000400500001-7 Secret u a as: ? Major Components As the regime's highest policymaking body, the Cu- ban Communist Party's 14-member Politburo theo- retically functions as the chief decisionmaking and oversight body for Havana's tightly controlled guerril- la support program. In practice, however, these re- sponsibilities fall to specific components of the larger Central Committee. the AD) is responsible for providing cohesion and direction to Cuba's "liberation" programs in Latin America and the Caribbean. Since June 1974, the AD has been headed by Manuel Pineiro Losada, a charter member of Cuba's guerrilla "elite" and a favorite of the Castro brothers.' Charged with undermining US influence in the region and supporting local liberation movements, Pineiro's organization operates largely behind the scenes. the AD, which we currently estimate has some 200 personnel, has conducted a variety of traditional intelligence activities such as penetration and agent-of-influence operations. The AD periodically conducts its activities openly, however, contacting other Communist or left- ist parties and personalities, disseminating official Cuban Communist Party propaganda, and providing support to exile groups in the host country or in Cuba. Nonetheless, the principal role of the AD, in our judgment, has been to coordinate Havana's provision of training, supplies, and funds to guerrilla organiza- tions and other radical leftist groups-actions that have touched most of the countries in this hemisphere. 25X1 25X1 25X1 25X1 it is within these departments that the party's operational plans are initially developed. Our research-docu- mented in appendix A and elsewhere in this paper- reveals, for example, the direct involvement of some half dozen senior Cuban officials in the orchestration of Havana's subversive activities in or from nearly every country in the Western Hemisphere and many countries in Africa. Moreover, it appears certain that such plans must first pass muster with Cuban Presi- dent and Party First Secretary Fidel Castro before rubberstamp approval is granted by the Politburo. It is at this point, in our opinion, that the responsible Central Committee department begins marshaling resources from within the Cuban Government to carry out a designated party program or plan of action. Policy Coordination and Implementation. the America Department of the Central Committee of the Cuban Communist Party (PCC/CC/AD, or simply The AD has traditionally been organized into at least four regional sections: North America, South Ameri- ca, Central America, and the Caribbean. More re- cently, however, this bureaucratic structure may have ' Prior to 1974, Cuba's "liberation" work was carried out by the National Liberation Department (NLD), which, by late 1961, had evolved into the General Intelligence Directorate (DGI) of the Interior Ministry (MININT). Pineiro, who was the first chief of the DGI, took personal charge of the activities of the NLD until late 1969, when he was given exclusive control of the newly formed Liberation Directorate (LD)-in effect, a MININT task force- now separated from the more "classical" overseas intelligence- collection-oriented DGI. Dissolution of the LD followed in June 1974, when Havana announced that the party's old department of foreign relations had been replaced by two new departments: the AD (under Pineiro), and a General Department responsible for affairs outside the Western Hemisphere. Lower oil earnings have caused a large shortfall in the foreign exchange earnings Baghdad needs this year to make large payments for goods imported on credit and to meet rescheduled debts to foreign lenders. To reduce the growing gap between revenues and expenditures, Iraq will have to cut 1986 imports and press creditors for further rescheduling of payments due this year. Iraq is looking to Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to increase their financial aid this year, but belt-tightening at home probably will prevent these countries from fully offsetting the decrease in Iraqi oil revenues. Payments Crunch in 1986 The slide in Iraqi oil revenues and foreign exchange reserves since 1982 has forced Baghdad to resort to deferred payments for nearly all civilian imports. Despite Iraq's financial difficulties, its trading partners had extended credit in anticipation of higher oil revenues from the Iraqi-Saudi pipeline that opened in October 1985. Sharply lower oil prices, however, have turned the tables on Baghdad and its creditors. Assuming a $15 per barrel aver- age oil price, we estimate Iraqi oil revenues will fall from $11.4 billion in 1985 to about $8.5 billion this year, even with an increase in oil exports of some 350,000 b/d. Iraqi oil exports are near capacity and cannot be increased substantially until mid-1987, when a second pipeline through Turkey is complet- ed. To adjust to lower oil revenues, we believe Iraq will have to slash imports by roughly 25 percent this year and, in addition, find a way to cut some $2.2- 2.7 billion of the $9 billion in payments-including civilian and military-due this year. Sudan's public-sector econo- my, on whose payrolls and subsidies many political- ly vocal urban Sudanese depend, is rapidly going bankrupt, the victim of diminished donor assistance and failed government policies. Meanwhile, Sudan's unofficial economy continues to thrive, but has come under increasing assault by the regime and may be less able to cushion the population from commodity shortages in the future. While the new government will undoubtedly attempt to tackle the many severe economic problems facing Sudan, we doubt that it will be strong enough or capable enough to redirect the economy, or enforce belt- tightening. Failure to reach agreement with the IMF over an acceptable economic reform package, together with the dim prospects of reducing arrears-which had reached $244 million by January 1986-led to Sudan's formal exclusion in February from access to IMF resources. In practical terms, the IMF decision has changed very little in the relationship; Khartoum had been effectively barred from tap- ping IMF resources from the moment that arrears began to accrue in July 1984. Meanwhile, consulta- tions between the Fund and Sudanese officials will continue, unaffected by the ineligibility declara- tion. The prospects for Sudan being able to imple- ment an IMF-endorsed reform package in the near future are remote, however. The government is simply too weak to perform the control functions that an IMF program would require. Paris Club rescheduling of official debt and Lon- don Club rescheduling of commercial debt is also likely to become more difficult in the absence of an IMF accord. Nonetheless, such rescheduling exer- cises are becoming increasingly irrelevant as Sudan's debt service capability continues to de- cline. Largely for political and humanitarian reasons, most major donors are likely to continue to disburse financial aid, albeit at reduced levels. The type of aid, however, will probably be influenced at least partially by the level of commitment the new regime displays toward economic reform. If, as seems likely, the new government remains wedded to astate-dominated economy, some donors may choose to limit direct balance-of-payments support. Project-related assistance, on the other hand, will probably continue. Recent Policy Moves Domestic policy initiatives pursued by the outgoing transitional government either have proved ineffec- tual, or have set the stage for further serious problems. Budgetary measures announced over the past several months have largely centered around increasing government revenue through closing tax loopholes and instituting new taxes. Most of these measures will generate much less revenue than anticipated because the government is not strong enough to enforce these regulations effectively. Aside from the problems of lax enforcement and corruption, the government's control, for the most part, extends only slightly beyond the outskirts of Khartoum and the Gezira region to the south. Beyond this narrow corridor, smuggling and black markets financed through illegal foreign exchange transactions dominate the economy. The IMF declaration may have convinced many donors that any meaningful resolution of Sudan's debt problems is impossible, thereby affecting their willingness to provide the level and type of financial support Sudanese officials have come to expect. Under these circumstances, little progress, or even failure, is likely given the wide gap between exporters' and importers' interests. An Agreement in Trouble The six-year-old rubber accord-sponsored by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Develop- ment and designed to stabilize natural rubber prices-is the youngest of the market-intervention commodity pacts and, like the others, has been largely ineffectual. Although natural rubber prices have recovered somewhat in the first three months of 1986, they are still more than 40 percent below peak 1980 levels. Moreover, rubber price fluctua- tions have not been reduced appreciably. Indeed, despite buffer stock purchases, the International Rubber Organization (INRO), which administers the pact, has twice had to revise its price band downward-the last time by 3 percent last August. Moreover, the large quantity of rubber in the official INRA stockpile-about 360,000 metric tons or roughly one-tenth of annual non-Commu- nist usage-is having a depressing effect on prices. Currently, foreign tax laws offer firms no greater competitive advantage than US laws, but the financial and capital characteristics of foreign firms provide them significant tax savings. Foreign electronics firms reap large tax advantages from their greater diversification and use of debt. The past losses of many European auto companies will shelter them from taxes for the next several years, while all foreign automakers, except Toyota, benefit from their heavy use of debt. Although corporate tax- ation is more frequently a function of the political strength of domestic industries and government revenue requirements than international competi- tiveness, governments have actively encouraged various activities such as regional development and high-technology industry through the tax code. Moreover, recent tax measures-implemented or contemplated-by industrial countries threaten to restore the tax advantage that the foreign competi- tors of US firms enjoyed before 1981. Mature High-Technology Industry. Our analysis of corporate tax burdens on examples of mature and high-technology industries-automobiles and electronics, respectively-indicates that, on aver- age, West European firms (except West German) in both sectors have sharply lower while Japanese firms face comparable or higher tax burdens than those in the United States. High-technology com- panies, however-particularly those in Japan and the United States-argue that the tax code is biased against them because it fails to account for their special characteristics and investments: ? Depreciation provisions favor capital-intensive in- dustries and fail to account for the rapid obsole- sence of high-technology investments. ? The preferential tax treatment accorded debt favors less risky investments. ? Inadequate tax-loss provisions reduce the impact of tax incentives designed to encourage investment. Our analysis indicates that, in practice, foreign electronics and automobile firms are on a more equal tax footing than those in the United States. This equality results largely from the greater diver- sification of foreign electronics firms and differing financial practices rather than less biased tax sys- tems. US electronics firms tend to have higher tax burdens than US automobile firms because they are more labor intensive, invest relatively more in structures (compared to equipment), and finance a greater portion of investments with internal funds rather than debt. Depreciation systems in France, Japan, and West Germany are no more neutral than the current US capital recovery system. Foreign electronics firms, however, are more diversified than US electronics firms, and have capital structures very similar to their counterparts in the automobile industry. As a result, foreign electronics firms are less subject to the bias favoring capital-intensive sectors conferred by accelerated depreciation. Even this gap may narrow because of the increasing capital intensity of US semiconductor firms and the proposed elimi- nation of the US investment tax credit. On an overall basis, most foreign firms reap a large tax advantage through their extensive use of debt financing. z The ability of Japanese electronics firms, for example, to operate with higher debt levels than their US counterparts may provide Among foreign firms, Toyota is one of the few exceptions to the heavy use of debt. Some analysts have suggested that Toyota avoids the use of debt in order to reduce its susceptibility to government pressures to hold back exports or restrain its domestic market share. Growth of energy production also slowed, with crude oil and coal up only 2 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively. The first-quarter slowdown continues a trend of cooling industrial production caused by controls-particularly credit restraints-imposed a year ago and by energy shortages. Industrial output increased at a 10-percent annual rate in the fourth quarter last year, and Chinese officials announced at the recent National People's Congress that the target would be 8 percent in 1986. China's Nuclear China announced that the Ministry of Nuclear Industry (MNI) will take over Ministry Takes Charge responsibility from the Ministry of Water Resources and Electric Power of Guangdong Plant (MWREP) for the proposed nuclear project at Guangdong. MWREP had overseen the project through negotiations with the French and British for reactors and generators, respectively, that led to letters of intent signed last month. Foreign exchange and budget constraints have forced Beijing to emphasize the development of domestic nuclear technology-an MNI proto- type nuclear plant is being built near Shanghai-instead of the expensive plant imports MWREP favors. MNI's takeover of the Guangdong plant will consolidate China's reduced nuclear program under one ministry but might cause delays in negotiations. MNI's enhanced role may also hold promise for the United States for at least small-scale nuclear cooperation and sales- MNI's plant design is based on US technology. MNI officials in the past have been more responsive to cooperation with the United States than have their MWREP counterparts. China Holds China's first trade fair for technology exports, held in Shenzhen 10-20 April, First Technology provides an unusual opportunity for foreigners to view advanced Chinese Export Fair products and signaled Beijing's determination to markedly expand its technol- ogy sales. The fair showcased 1,700 items in areas such as nuclear energy, electronics, aviation, astronautics, and defense, many of which were regarded as confidential until recently, according to the Chinese press. Satellite launching technology and civilian applications of nuclear technology were the star attractions, but foreign observers considered many of the exhibits-which included herbal medicines and garments-far from advanced. Some 200 Moroccans living in the western Algerian city of Oran have been arrested and more than 300 other Moroccans have been deported. Rabat will almost certainly soon retaliate in like manner. The official Algerian media assert that those being expelled are illegal residents. however, the Algerians are in fact confiscating permits from Moroccan workers and then expelling them. A press report from Rabat indicates the deportations began on December 11, the same day Moroccan troops were officially welcomed in the Saharan capital of El Aaiun. Algeria's harassment tactics have alarmed the estimated 350,000 Moroccans living in Algeria. Algiers may continue these tactics on a selective basis, but probably will not attempt to expel the entire Moroccan community. The press reports also speculated that the South Africans raised the matter of opening a consulate in Abidjan. The visit falls within the context of President Houphouet-Boigny's determination to encourage a dialogue with Pretoria and the exchange of visitors. Last month, for instance, the Ivorian information minister paid a much-publicized visit to South Africa. When querried about the possibility of a South African consulate in Abidjan, one Ivorian foreign ministry official said he thought the establishment of relations with South Africa was a "certainty" and would come "very soon." The US embassy believes, however, that the Ivorians are likely to proceed cautiously in moving toward closer ties with Pretoria because of the adverse publicity being given to South Africa's role in Angola and the mounting criticism of South Africa by members of the Organization of African Unity. In discussing landing rights, one Ivorian official would go no further than to say that the matter was "being worked out" for South African Airways. This contrasts sharply with remarks to the press by a member of the South African delegation on returning to Pretoria, who said that all obstacles to regular use of Abidjan "had been removed." One Western diplomat in Abidjan also reports that an actual agreement had been negotiated. With the OAU's continent-wide trade union affiliate call- ing once again on all African countries to ban flights of foreign aircraft to and from South Africa, it would be surprising if Ivory Coast had chosen this time to grant landing right to South African plans. review_required.title: La madurez de Miguel de Cervantes : una vida en la Corte (1580-1604)
review_required.creator: Lucía Megías, José Manuel, author
description: 396 pages : 24 cm

En su segundo volumen de la biografia Miguel de Cervantes, el catedratico Jose Manuel Lucia Megias situa a Cervantes a su vuelta del cautiverio de Argel. Se gana la vida como funcionario de la corte. Es en terminos de la epoca un "solicitador de causas". Entre sus tareas contrastadas figuran la de ser discreto correo real en Oran, comisario de abastos, cobrador de impuestos, "juez ejecutor de su Majestad", ayudante de edicion para el librero Francisco de Robles, contable y, a ratos, escritor en busca de nuevos retos. La leyenda dice que fue en la carcel, que lo acogio varias veces, donde mayor sosiego encontro para sus aficiones literarias. En estos veinticinco anos tambien tuvo tiempo de tener amores con Ana Franca, reconocer a su hija natural Isabel de Saavedra y casarse en Esquivias con Catalina de Salazar. De 1580 a 1605 Cervantes publica algunos poemas, la novela pastoril de La Galatea, compuso mas de veinte o treinta comedias recibidas con "general y gustoso aplauso" y da a la imprenta el exitoso libro de El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha. Se hallaba, en enemistad manifiesta con Lope de Vega, cuando de nuevo fue apresado por su improbable implicacion en la muerte del caballero Gaspar de Ezpeleta, asesinado delante de la casa que ocupaba toda la familia Cervantes en Valladolid
Includes bibliographical references (pages 377-383) and indexes

review_required.creator: Lendler, Marc

Does the political thinking of ordinary citizens change during periods of crisis? Marc Lendler addresses this question by investigating the story behind an unusually prolonged and ultimately successful strike - a five-year conflict at the Colt Firearms Company in Hartford, Connecticut, in the 1980s. ARTICLE APPIi ( 1`IGMI I VRI\ 111'ICJ ON PAGE 21 January 1986 Letters The Lessons of the Richard Nixon Case To the Editor: I should like to comment on "Les- sons of the Alger Hiss Case" (Op-Ed, Jan. 8), described as having been adapted from a speech delivered last tall by former President Nixon. Mr. Nixon's article prompts me to deny again the charges that provided the basis for his speech. My case has often been trotted out to justify reactionary policies far re- moved from the issues of the case it- self, and Mr. Nixon once again tries to make it a connecting thread for his views on a number of world and do- mestic events. At this time, I shall leave to others the correction of Mr. Nixon's biased views on those general subjects he has dragged in. I shall concern myself here only with the reasons that support my innocence and the invalidity of my conviction. My case was tried In the hysteria of the early cold-war year of 1949 after sensational hearings by the House Committee an Un-American Activi- ties. Richard M. Nixon did indeed take a prominent part in those hear- ings and in fomenting the public prejudice hanging over my two trials. Ever since, he has made political capital of his role in my case. Despite that prejudice and the im- proper tactics of the prosecution, the jury in my first trial could not reach a verdict. Years later, in the aftermath of Watergate, Congress strengthened the Freedom of Information Act, which enabled me in 1975 to seek Fed- eral Bureau of Investigation and other documents that would disclose the tactics used by the prosecution. Delays and flat denials met my ef. forts. Nevertheless, by 1978, I had ob? tained sufficient documents to war- rant filing a petition for a writ of error to overturn my conviction. Those documents showed that the prosecu- tion had withheld exculpatory evi- dence, misled the judge and jury on the identity and authenticity of the typewriter that was the crucial ex- hibit in the case and committed other transgressions. Those documents have been pub- lished in facsimile by Hill & Wang in two volumes. Anyone can examine this proof of my assertion that the conviction was a miscarriage of jus- tice. The issue presented is one of fact and common-sense judgment. Any reader can determine whether or not to agree with the judge, him- self a Nixon appointee, who denied my petition. Once more, I assert that I did not engage in espionage. It is still simply Whittaker Chambers's word against mine. In calmer times my word has been accepted, and it will be again. My case seems to be a barometer of the cold war. I resent, in particular, Mr. Nixon's insinuation, with no basis except Chambers's word, that my late wife engaged in wrongdoing. This seems to me to be of a piece with his prac- tices through the long years since his membership in the House Committee on Un-American Activities in 1948. Perhaps this latest impropriety helps to point up the lessons of the Richard Nixon case. ALGER HISS New York, Jan. 9, 1986 Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2010/07/21 : CIA-RDP90-00552R000302660001-5

all_retained_discoveries.title: Profiles In History: Autograph Auction 34 Fall 2002
all_retained_discoveries.creator: Profiles in History
all_retained_discoveries.description: Profiles in History: Autograph Auction 34 Winter 2002 Auction Highlights include: Erwin Rommel's raw, triumphant postcard sent on the literal opening week of WWII. Harry Truman's unedited reflections on brawling with Stalin and Churchill at Potsdam. Daniel Boone's hand-drawn Kentucky boundary logs. FDR's localized 1927 ballot where he hand-wrote Eleanor Roosevelt into local office. Presidential & Foundational Era John Adams (December 10, 1799): An exceptionally rare official letter signed as President to the U.S. Senate. Adams explicitly praises the promptitude and zeal of federal troops used to crush the Fries Rebellion in eastern Pennsylvania. The catalog highlights a fascinating backstory: local farmers revolted over direct property taxes passed to fund defense against France. While Adams declared the riot a "highhanded" dangerous affair, he determined it wasn't treason and eventually issued a full pardon—a move that cost him critical support from his own conservative Federalist Party during the tight election of 1800. John Quincy Adams (June 6, 1791): A rare early autograph letter signed to a legal colleague named "Putnam". Written right after his admission to the bar, Adams coordinates a legal writ before playfully adding that the intricate question posed to him is too perplexing for a busy day, proposing they instead discuss it soon over "a segar [cigar] & glass of wine". John Quincy Adams Stock Certificate (April 17, 1809): An original stock certificate for the Boylston Market Association, signed by Adams as its very first president. The historic market complex was built far out of town at the time and named after Adams' second cousin, Ward Nicholas Boylston. James Bowdoin (March 30, 1786): An important Revolutionary War-era letter signed as Governor of Massachusetts to the Governor of North Carolina. Bowdoin officially states that Massachusetts has acceded to Virginia's proposal to hold the Annapolis Convention in Maryland to regulate interstate trade. This meeting ultimately served as the critical precursor to the 1787 Philadelphia Convention, where the weak Articles of Confederation were discarded in favor of the U.S. Constitution. James Buchanan (March 13, 1859): An exceptional pre-Civil War letter signed as President to Indian Affairs Commissioner James Denver. Buchanan voices deep gratitude for Denver's firm, impartial leadership as the territorial Governor of Kansas during the incredibly violent "Bleeding Kansas" border wars. Millard Fillmore (September 15, 1869): A handwritten letter showing a warm kinship between two U.S. presidents. Fillmore writes to voice his deep relief that the newly inaugurated Chief Executive, Ulysses S. Grant, had returned home safely and was on the path to recovering his health after an unexpected illness forced him to miss the New York State Fair. James A. Garfield (April 15, 1881): An exceptionally rare official letter of state signed as President. Garfield authorizes the Secretary of State to affix the Seal of the United States to his formal reply to a congratulatory message from the Republic of San Marino. Because Garfield was tragically shot by an assassin just two and a half months later, documents signed during his brief 6-month presidency are of immense rarity. James A. Garfield on Lincoln's Funeral (May 2, 1865): A poignant handwritten letter written as a Representative from Ohio to Speaker of the House Schuyler Colfax. Garfield writes from his home state to describe traveling to Cleveland to meet Abraham Lincoln’s slow-moving funeral train. He expresses deep regret that Colfax was unable to accompany the cortege, creating an incredible historical link between the first and second U.S. presidents to be assassinated. Andrew Jackson Walking Cane Letter (c. January/February 1831): An exceptional letter signed as President to a Virginia resident, typed out by his adopted son. Jackson warmly accepts a presentation walking cane carved from a tree that stood on the physical battlefield of the Battle of New Orleans. Jackson praises the brave men whose valor served as the "Security of the Union," referencing the legendary War of 1812 victory that vaulted his military persona into the White House. Andrew Jackson Land Grant (January 1, 1830): A document signed as President on vellum, granting a 113-acre plot of land located near St. Louis, Missouri. Thomas Jefferson & the UVA Rotunda (October 7, 1823): A magnificent autograph letter signed from Monticello to Master Carpenter James Oldham. Writing as the "Father of the University of Virginia," the aging former president outlines the ongoing construction of the university's famous architectural crown jewel, the UVA Rotunda. Jefferson rejects Oldham’s direct financial appeals to the Board of Visitors regarding a wage dispute, telling him that contractual adjustments must go through the executive proctor or the ordinary courts. This exact letter famously triggered the very first lawsuit brought against the University of Virginia. Thomas Jefferson Navy Commission (March 16, 1807): An exceptional document signed as President (countersigned by Navy Secretary Robert Smith) commissioning Hethcote J. Reed as a Lieutenant. Reed served as a midshipman on the historic frigate USS Constitution ("Old Ironsides") during the Barbary Coast patrols and fought in the celebrated assault on Tripoli during the Tripolitan War. Thomas Jefferson & James Madison Ships' Papers (December 30, 1806): A large folio-sized safe-passage document signed jointly by Jefferson as President and Madison as Secretary of State. The document features a rare four-language parallel text configuration (English, Dutch, French, and Spanish) granting passage to a brig carrying livestock and lumber out of an American port. William Henry Harrison Political Overtures (July 12, 1837): A dense, 4-page political strategy letter written to Whig organizer Silas M. Stilwell. Harrison plots with party allies Daniel Webster and Henry Clay to overthrow the Jacksonian Democrats in the upcoming 1840 election. Harrison warns his party to respect their opponents' perfect discipline, delivering a timeless political axiom: "Confidence in the weakness of our enemy has produced the most disastrous defeats on record." John F. Kennedy Handwritten Note (January 10, 1962): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed as President on official green White House stationery. Writing to a former Senate colleague ("Senator Martin"), Kennedy sends friendly New Year's greetings, marking one of only a handful of full one-page handwritten presidential letters from JFK in private hands. Herbert Hoover Signed Portrait (Undated): A handsome sepia portrait photograph of the smartly dressed president, warmly inscribed to a local doctor. Herbert Hoover anti-FDR Rant (September 3, 1934): A scathing 2-page typed letter attacking the newly formed "American Liberty League". Hoover accuses the disgruntled corporate Democrats backing the league of hijacking the 1932 Republican platform, bluntly declaring that he has no more confidence in their Wall Street model of liberty than the New Deal model. Herbert Hoover Teapot Dome Speech (November 14, 1933): A signed 5-page transcript of the speech Hoover delivered at the dedication of the Warren G. Harding Memorial. Hoover fiercely castigates the corrupt Teapot Dome conspirators for violating public trust. Historically, Teapot Dome ringleader Harry M. Daugherty sat seething barely thirty feet away in the audience as Hoover spoke. James Madison War-Date Letter (January 5, 1813): A superb presidential letter written marked "private" to his newly elected Vice President, Elbridge Gerry. Madison answers technical questions regarding taking the constitutional oath of office. He urges the aging Gerry to travel south to Virginia to avoid the harsh winter weather, writing: "Your friends in Virginia will then be the gainers..." The catalog highlights that Gerry followed Madison's advice and took his oath at home in Cambridge before taking his seat as president pro tempore of the Senate. This letter is also famous for detailing the origin of the term "gerrymander," coined after Gerry distorted Massachusetts voting districts to look like a salamander. James Madison Cabinet Strife Letter (August 29, 1810): A fascinating autograph letter signed as President to his bitter political rival, Senator Samuel Smith. Madison handles tense complaints regarding Treasury deposits and defends his embattled Treasury Secretary, Albert Gallatin. This letter captures a highly unstable moment in Madison's administration, balancing a divided cabinet alongside a deteriorating relationship with Napoleon on the brink of the War of 1812. James Madison Ship's Passport (June 1, 1811): A scallop-top ship's passport signed on vellum by President Madison, countersigned by Secretary of State Robert Smith, granting safe passage to a two-gun schooner named the Fly of Bristol. James K. Polk Grandfather Vindication (August 24, 1844): A handwritten campaign letter marked "Private" to a Nashville editor. Polk fiercely defends against toxic Whig character attacks that accused his grandfather, Col. Ezekiel Polk, of being a Revolutionary War Tory (a British loyalist). Polk biography notes that Polk became entirely obsessed with this issue, spending more energy defending his grandfather's memory than almost any other topic in the tight 1844 election. Franklin D. Roosevelt Scripture Beliefs (January 6, 1929): A typed letter written as Governor of New York to a Texas reverend, explicitly confirming his deep reliance on the Bible: "Please understand that I read the Scriptures and believe in the Book from cover to cover, and am trying to carry out the teaching of the Master as best I can." Franklin D. Roosevelt Disabled Veterans Message (December 24, 1935): A moving typed letter signed as President, delivered on Christmas Eve to a World War I veterans organization. Roosevelt praises the noble living and noble dead, offering the everlasting gratitude of the nation they served. Franklin D. Roosevelt Dutchess County Absentee Ballot (November 8, 1927): An extraordinary legal voting archive completed and signed three times by FDR just before his election as Governor of New York. Voting an all-Democrat ticket, Roosevelt casts a vote against the extension of the New York Governor's term (a historic irony given he would later break all boundaries by winning four terms as President). Best of all, on the local town section, Roosevelt explicitly hand-writes in his wife, Eleanor Roosevelt, as School Director for Hyde Park. Eleanor Roosevelt on Joseph P. Kennedy (June 21): A rare handwritten letter signed as First Lady to her son James. Eleanor recounts hosting a porch picnic lunch for the Kennedy family patriarch, Joseph P. Kennedy, leaving a sharp and incredibly shrewd historical assessment of the future ambassador: "Joe Kennedy has been here... I enjoyed listening to him. A complete egotist but an intelligent & kindly one." Harry S. Truman on Potsdam & McCarthy (May 28, 1954): A spectacular 6-page autograph letter signed "Harry" to his former Secretary of State, Dean Acheson. Truman recounts working on his memoirs 17 hours a day and relives an exasperated clash he had at the Potsdam Conference with Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin regarding Spanish dictator Francisco Franco. He tells Acheson that he snapped at the dictators, declaring he didn't come to Berlin to run a "police court". When translated, Stalin roared with laughter and suggested they talk about Poland instead. Truman then transitions to domestic affairs, bluntly observing that the ongoing Sen. Joseph McCarthy anti-communist hearings are causing massive shame to his Republican friends. He sharply criticizes the Eisenhower White House as "smart but inexperienced boys" who are upsetting NATO and throwing away America's military strength while dangerously eyeing intervention in Indo-China. Harry S. Truman on JFK & the 1960 Convention (July 9, 1960): Another remarkable handwritten letter signed "Harry" to Dean Acheson, penned just two days before the 1960 Democratic National Convention. Truman writes that party leaders are begging him to attend, adding that he intends to "have a lot of fun with the guessers and the prophets." The catalog notes that Truman strongly disliked John F. Kennedy, previously calling him too inexperienced and publicly demanding: "Senator, are you certain that you are quite ready for the country?" Woodrow Wilson on the British Blockade (March 19, 1915): A typed letter signed as President, accompanied by a hand-corrected 4-page Letter of State addressed to Great Britain regarding their aggressive naval blockade off Germany. Wilson warns the British government that their unusually massive shipping cordon violates international law by burdening neutral American merchantmen. This warning was terrifyingly on-point: just two weeks later, the German navy retaliated against the blockade zone, sinking the passenger liner Lusitania and drowning nearly 200 Americans. Woodrow Wilson Literature Quote (October 16, 1899): A beautiful, signed autograph quote penned while serving as the President of Princeton University: "Literature is a thing of convictions, of insights, of what is felt and seen and heard and hoped for."Zachary Taylor (June 19, 1850): An incredibly rare letter signed as President, written to New York Governor Hamilton Fish less than one month before Taylor's sudden death in office. Taylor declines an invitation to the New York State Fair, noting that he cannot leave Washington while Congress is aggressively debating the highly controversial Compromise of 1850 regarding the extension of slavery. Taylor fell ill five days after July 4th and passed away from rampaging cholera. William H. Taft on the League of Nations (December 18, 1920): A typed letter signed regarding a controversy over the omission of any reference to God in the preamble to the League of Nations' charter. Taft notes he would have strongly favored a recognition of the Deity, but argues that the omission wasn't sinister and doesn't justify a big debate, concluding: "Preambles are not the substance of the League, and it is about the substance that we are interested." Civil War, Military, & Global Affairs Jefferson Davis (March 20, 1863): A high-stakes Civil War-date letter signed as President of the C.S.A. to Georgia Governor J.E. Brown. Davis addresses a tense military incident where Confederate General Braxton Bragg ordered his quartermasters to use armed force, if necessary, to seize control of Georgia's state-owned Western & Atlantic Railroad after transit workers allegedly refused to transport Southern munitions. Davis acts as an urgent diplomat, regretting the general's extra-legal threats and smoothing over state-versus-federal tensions with a plea for Southern solidarity. Turner Ashby (February 29, 1862): A highly scarce Confederate army receipt signed by Ashby as Colonel in Winchester, Virginia, securing transport wagons and horses. Ashby was one of "Stonewall" Jackson's most trusted cavalry subordinates and was tragically killed in action just three months later. Ellis Spear of the 20th Maine (Undated): A fascinating 5-page original autograph manuscript recounting the close-quarters horrors of the 1864 Wilderness Campaign and the Battle of Spotsylvania Court House. Spear, who took command of the legendary regiment after Joshua Chamberlain was promoted, reflects on the exhausting night marches and constant skirmishes that were enough to make a veteran tired just thinking about it decades later. Joshua L. Chamberlain & Thomas D. Chamberlain (October 12, 1870): A unique historical check filled out by the "Savior of Gettysburg" and signed jointly by both famous brothers. Thomas served as a captain under Joshua, and famously survived a near-fatal close-range gun encounter while successfully securing the Union's left flank on Little Round Top. William F. Smith (March 11, 1891): A candid post-war letter where the former Union Major General admits he is writing a defense paper to evaluate the battlefield performance of General Grant. Smith controversially concludes that General Grant was a poor military commander compared to Confederate generals, echoing a highly unpopular public opinion at the time. Edward Townsend (March 30, 1865): An official State Department invitation presented to the Governor of Missouri to witness the historic flag-raising ceremony at Fort Sumter. Scheduled for April 14, 1865—exactly four years to the day after the fort fell—the event allowed General Robert Anderson to re-raise the very same tattered garrison flag that had marked the literal start of the Civil War. David Ben-Gurion (March 13, 1954): A powerful letter handwritten in Hebrew from his retreat in Sde Boker to a Knesset member. Ben-Gurion issues a stark warning to "naive" pacifists, declaring that Israel must rid itself of illusions that external Jewish organizations can guarantee safety from border raids, fiercely arguing that the sole security of Israel lies with the IDF. Catherine the Great (January 9, 1793): A beautiful, tender New Year's greeting letter written in French by the Russian Empress to her sister, the Princess of Anhalt-Zerbst. Abraham Lincoln Legal Opinion (August 17, 1850): A full-page autograph letter signed from Springfield, Illinois, regarding a civil land title dispute. Evaluating a forged property deed, Lincoln delivers a characteristically blunt and succinct legal assessment: "This is the whole story — The case can not be gained by much talking." Abraham Lincoln Circuit Court Receipt (May 1, 1858): A handwritten financial document signed as an Illinois general practice attorney. Dated just six weeks before his famous "House Divided" speech propelled him to national visibility, Lincoln signs off on court fees received for a case in the Vermilion Circuit Court. Robert E. Lee Lexington Correspondence (June 22, 1866): A gracious 2-page letter written as President of Washington College to a former Union soldier, Major Richard P. Hammond. Writing just one year after the war ended, Lee attempts to track down a missing Confederate general on behalf of his former battlefield adversary, showcasing the smooth, respectful resumption of peace between North and South. Robert E. Lee Signature (March 8, 1869): A bold, clean ink signature reading "R.E. Lee," clipped from a larger document. John Hancock Military Appointment (July 1, 1775): A spectacular Revolutionary War document signed boldly by Hancock as President of the Continental Congress, countersigned by Charles Thomson. Hancock appoints an ensign to the Massachusetts Regiment just two weeks after the bloody Battle of Bunker Hill, and a mere two days before George Washington arrived in Cambridge to assume formal command of the Continental Army. Julia Ward Howe Battle Hymn of the Republic Manuscript (March 21, 1865): A monumental piece of American cultural history. A complete 2-page autograph manuscript of her famous Union rallying anthem, written entirely in her hand and signed just two weeks before Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Incredibly, this specific copy features an un-published extra stanza attacking god's contemners that did not make it into the final Atlantic Monthly printing. Francis Gary Powers U-2 Spy Flight Letter (September 22, 1970): A rare typed letter signed by the famous Cold War pilot to an aviation magazine editor. Powers reviews a book tracking the history of aerial reconnaissance, commenting on the super-secret CIA U-2 program that caused an international crisis when he was shot down over downtown Moscow in 1960. Theodor Herzl Zionist Letter (August 10, 1902): A printed political letter signed by the zionist leader from Vienna. Written right as critical negotiations with the Ottoman Empire collapsed, Herzl outlines the upcoming agenda for the Zionist Action Committee, which marked his historic shift to lobby the British government for a Jewish homeland. Nathaniel Lyon Pre-Battle Report (May 12, 1861): An exceptionally rare Civil War letter written from the St. Louis Arsenal just three months before Lyon was killed in action. Writing to the Adjutant General, Lyon reports on a local clash where Union troops and a civilian mob engaged in a deadly shootout, killing 12 people. Lyon openly criticizes his brash superior, General William S. Harney, warning that Harney's erratic city orders painfully embarrass his covert strategy to stop pro-Confederate combinations from seizing the state of Missouri. Philip H. Sheridan Legendary War Horse Letter (March 24, 1876): A wonderful letter penned by the Union hero to an old army comrade. Sheridan reveals that the famous black horse he rode during his frantic, morale-boosting race from Winchester to rally his routed troops at the Battle of Cedar Creek is still alive and well in his possession, noting: "He looks almost as well now as when you saw him in Virginia." Sheridan later renamed the black horse "Winchester." George H. Thomas on the Fitz John Porter Court-Martial (January 5, 1870): An autograph letter signed by the Union general known as "The Rock of Chickamauga." Thomas comments on the infamous Civil War court-martial of Gen. Fitz John Porter, who was relieved of command for alleged dereliction of duty during the Battle of Groveton. Thomas defends Porter's character, stating he never believed Porter willfully neglected his duty. George Washington Free Frank (Undated): A prominent, large ink signature reading "Go: Washington," scrawled as a free-franked address panel to a Connecticut cobbler named Joseph Webb. Historical records indicate Washington wrote to Webb primarily to check on custom orders for "horse skin" boots. George Washington on Long Island Plundering (October 31, 1778): A superb Revolutionary War-date letter signed by the Commander-in-Chief from his headquarters in Fredericksburg. Washington issues a stern reprimand to a local major after learning that Continental scouts traveling to Long Island under the pretext of gathering intelligence were indiscriminately plundering and distressing the local inhabitants. Washington commands him to stop the pernicious practice, explicitly ordering him to only employ those as spies or observers in whom he can place proper confidence. Daniel Boone Fayette County Survey (May 15, 1785): A mind-bogglingly rare complete manuscript document written and signed by the legendary pioneer as a Deputy Surveyor in Fayette County, Kentucky. Boone hand-writes the boundary logs for a 1,000-acre land plot using uncorrected frontier misspellings, tracing lines from "2 Shuger trees" to a "white oke and hickory." Boone tragically lost almost all of his own land in this exact county three years later due to title disputes. Simon Kenton Frontier Warrant (Undated): A financial document signed by the famous trans-Allegheny frontiersman who famously saved Daniel Boone's life during an Indian raid at Boonesborough. Science, Discovery, & Literature Benjamin Franklin (April 9, 1773): A magnificent 2-page autograph letter signed and initialed from London to "Dear Jenky" (Jane Parker). Franklin musters his immense powers of diplomacy to resolve a delicate financial disagreement with the family of his deceased New York printing business partner. To preserve their long family tie, Franklin delivers a timeless piece of advice: "But I think it contributes to the Duration of Friendship to keep its Accounts, & those of Business distinct & separate; and that an exact Justice in Pounds Shillings & Pence should be observed between Friends as between Strangers." Albert Einstein "World State" Manuscript (Undated, Post-WWI): A monumental 3-page unsigned autograph manuscript written in green ink. Einstein maps out a bold political plan for a unified "World State", arguing that the League of Nations failed because member states refused to surrender their individual sovereignty. He argues that a global political system is unconditionally necessary to stop our planet from becoming unbearable for humans, while warning that intellectuals often fail in politics because they lack quick decision-making and human people skills. Tantalizingly, the top of the page features a series of Einstein's handwritten mathematical equations in electromagnetics. Albert Einstein Signed Portrait (1935): A classic black-and-white portrait of Einstein in a tuxedo, beautifully inscribed in German to friends in remembrance of "happy musical evenings" spent playing his beloved violin. John Flamsteed (June 29, 1695): A rare signed financial receipt from the historic first Astronomer Royal of England. Flamsteed's meticulous star mapping directly provided the data Sir Isaac Newton used to verify his legendary theory of gravity. Raymond Chandler (November 5, 1946): A typed letter to his famous Hollywood agent, H.N. Swanson. Written right as Chandler abandoned the stress of the movie studios for the quiet coast of La Jolla, he tracks short story publishing rights while jokingly describing himself as "a guy who never says one thing when four will do." Samuel Francis Smith (December 4, 1893): A wonderful letter from the composer of "My Country, 'Tis of Thee", hoping his anthem kindles a spirit of freedom worldwide. Smith shares a lively reflection on aging, quoting Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.'s birthday tribute to fellow hymn-writer Julia Ward Howe, noting that the human spirit can burn in perpetual youth if kept active. Herman Melville Defending Mardi (June 5, 1849): A magnificent 3-page autograph letter signed to his British publisher Richard Bentley (who would publish Moby-Dick two years later). Melville defends his new novel Mardi, which British critics had violently panned as too abstract and metaphysical, writing a timeless defense of the artist's mind: "But some of us scribblers, my Dear Sir, always have a certain something unmanageable in us, that bids us do this or that, and be done it must – hit or miss." He then reveals he is shifting ground away from the South Seas to write a plain, straightforward, amusing sea narrative with no metaphysics—his semi-autobiographical masterpiece, Redburn: His First Voyage. Melville letters are of legendary rarity. Claude Monet London Illness (March 14, 1901): A poignant 5-page letter handwritten in French on Savoy Hotel stationery to his wife. Monet gripes about a sudden illness that struck him down in London just as he was attempting one last creative effort to capture the Gothic spires of Westminster rising through the changing Thames fog, producing his legendary London Series of impressionist masterpieces. Franklin D. Roosevelt Founding the March of Dimes (April 7, 1927): A historic handwritten letter signed on legal stationery regarding the incorporation of the Georgia Warm Springs Foundation (later known nationwide as the March of Dimes). Paralyzed by polio, FDR details establishing the foundation as a non-profit rehabilitation center to help fellow polio victims find strength, creating one of his most enduring humanitarian health legacies. Jack London on The Call of the Wild (August 28, 1903): A mind-bogglingly rare autograph letter written in pencil to an early reader immediately following the publication of his masterpiece. London explains his creative structure for the novel, revealing his logic behind naming his legendary canine protagonist: "The only reason I named him Buck was that years before I had filed away among my notes as appropriate dog names ‘Buck’ & ‘Bright.’ ... I chose Buck – I guess because it was stronger than Bright." He beautifully adds: "We know little or nothing about what dogs think. But then we may conclude from their actions what their mental processes might be..." West Africa Slave Trade Uprising (January 15, 1808): A terrifying historical letter written by two slave traders aboard the Ship Hibernia near the St. Paul's River in Sierra Leone. Writing at the absolute peak of the Atlantic slave trade, they describe a massive, violent slave uprising where hundreds of local fighters descended upon their factory staging fort, plundering the stores, cutting the trader's hand, and forcing them to flee under cover of night. Letters detailing slave trade mutinies written directly from Africa are of immense historical scarcity. Hollywood, Sports, & Pop Culture Dwight D. Eisenhower (November 22, 1944): A deeply moving wartime letter written from Versailles to his wife, Mamie. The Supreme Allied Commander handles regular family business—enclosing $25 to help buy a durable Christmas gift for their son—before offering a somber look at the front lines: "Well sweet I’d like to think that this mess would be over soon... But the fighting and the dying go on – and the end is not yet. ‘Civilization’ is not pretty, when it resorts to war." Josephine Earp (March 3, 1929): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed by the wife of legendary gunfighter Wyatt Earp. Written just months after Wyatt's death, the former actress coordinates travel details while defending her late husband's untamed frontier legacy. Thomas Edison on Theodore Roosevelt (April 1919): An original autograph note scrawled on a poem written by a 13-year-old girl honoring the late President. Edison writes in pencil: "Some Girl! It’s in the blood capacity for high mental action accompanies the germ plasm..." 1951 Brooklyn Dodgers Signed Baseball: An official ball signed by 22 legendary members of the team, including Chuck Dressen, Gil Hodges, Pee Wee Reese, and Jackie Robinson. This historic ball dates to the exact, infamous season that culminated in Ralph Branca giving up the pennant-winning "Shot Heard 'Round the World" home run to the rival Giants. Ty Cobb Batting Advice Letter (September 14, 1954): A massive 5-page strategy letter written in green ink by "The Georgia Peach" to Pirates manager Fred Haney. Cobb offers dense, un-asked-for advice to pull a struggling hitter out of a slump, detailing exact hand placements, swinging parallels, and a warning to stop swinging for the fences. Cooperstown Hall of Fame Signed Bat: An official souvenir baseball bat signed boldly on the barrel by 13 legendary titans, including Ted Williams, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, Hank Aaron, and a highly controversial addition by Pete Rose. Irving Berlin Signed Sheet Music (1938): Vintage sheet music for "Alexander's Ragtime Band", beautifully inscribed by Berlin to fellow Academy Award-nominated Hollywood film composer Lew Pollack. Lucille Ball (Undated): A gorgeous sepia publicity photograph featuring her resting elegantly on a ship's helm, signed with warm sentiments. Josephine Baker (1935): A spectacular, oversized vintage photograph of the exotic stage dancer captured mid-performance, signed with a bold French inscription. P.T. Barnum (November 30, 1887): A beautiful letter written to a young boy, where the legendary showman lovingly promises that his traveling circus, "The Greatest Show on Earth", will be even larger, funnier, and more marvelous next year. George Gershwin An American in Paris Photograph (March 1929): An extraordinary sepia portrait showing the legendary composer seated at his piano. In the lower margin, Gershwin beautifully pens an autograph musical quotation consisting of four bars of music, mapping out the famous primary orchestral theme of An American in Paris just three months after its Carnegie Hall debut. Ira Gershwin MGM Movie Contract (December 27, 1949): A historic 6-page studio contract signed by the legendary lyricist for the Academy Award-winning MGM musical An American in Paris. The contract maps out his $56,250 pay structure and includes the famous studio "morals and conduct" clause used to keep contract players under the studio's thumb. John F. Kennedy & Robert Frost Inaugural Booklet (April 1961): A unique presentation copy of the limited-edition booklet printed for Robert Frost’s White House reception. It features Frost's dedication poem alongside the full text of JFK's historic "Ask not what your country can do for you" speech. It is signed by Kennedy on the cover and features a warm inscription from Frost to a journalist friend detailing the plane flight they shared. Ernest Hemingway Overseas Background Check (Undated): A jovial letter handwritten entirely in pencil to his hunting buddy Charles Thompson—the direct inspiration for "Karl" in The Green Hills of Africa. Hemingway requests that Thompson serve as a character witness for a government background check so he can travel overseas, writing with his signature wit: "If they interrogate you you can tell them what a good patriot, swell guy, always pay my debts (within two years or 20)..."Jerome Kern Signed Sheet Music (May 19, 1938): Vintage sheet music for the song "You Couldn't Be Cuter", inscribed to fellow film composer Lew Pollack. It is accompanied by a funny typed letter where Kern jokes that the song will probably be a "mummy by Decoration Day". Alex Haley Roots Inscription (June 25, 1984): A signed card featuring a good-natured sentiment referencing his ground-breaking saga, sending brotherly love from "Chicken George" and the family of Kunta Kinte. California Gold Rush Prospector Letter (July 25, 1849): A fascinating 3-page letter written by early 49er Mason R. Packer from Stockton, California, to his wife back east. Packer notes the exorbitant prices of basic goods in the boomtowns and coordinates his departure for the gold diggings near Sutter's Fort. The Honeymooners Cast Signed Photograph: A vintage publicity still showing the four core cast members (Jackie Gleason, Audrey Meadows, Art Carney, and Joyce Randolph) hanging out of a New York City bus window, signed beautifully by each actor. Charles Lindbergh Aviation Matte Portrait (Undated): A striking, oversized sepia waist-up portrait captured by Underwood & Underwood, showing Lindbergh standing proudly with the Spirit of St. Louis in the background, signed cleanly on the photographer's matte. Charles Lindbergh Leather Flight Portrait (Undated): A magnificent head-and-shoulders sepia portrait showing the youthful aviator clad in his complete leather flight jacket, helmet, and goggles, signed in bold black ink. Both Lindbergh portraits originated directly from the estate of the nation's very first federal aviation regulator, William P. MacCracken. The Little Rascals Vintage Signatures (1938–1939): A rare and highly desirable collector's set of five individual autograph leaves signed by the core childhood stars of the fabled Hal Roach Our Gang comedies, including Spanky McFarland, Buckwheat, Alfalfa, Darla Hood, and Porky Lee. Willie Mosconi Signed Billiard Ball Set: A complete presentation box containing fifteen individual billiard balls and an accompanying cue ball, each signed in full by the perennial 15-time world champion. The catalog notes his historic 1954 exhibition record where he sank an unbelievable 526 consecutive pool balls without a single miss. George S. Patton Cadet Letters (c. Fall 1903): A beautiful early letter written as a young cadet attending the Virginia Military Institute (VMI) to his aunt. Exhibiting his lifelong obsession with historical military tactics, the future general explicitly asks her to bring him white writing paper (rejecting blue paper as un-military) along with a newly published textbook entitled Strategy as Illustrated in British Campaigns. Richard Nixon Anti-Communist Speech (c. April 1953): A massive 15-page original typed speech layout containing extensive handwritten corrections and segregation notes by Vice President Richard Nixon. Plunging into a aggressive defense of his controversial role hunting down hidden Communists on the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), Nixon defends the Alger Hiss investigations and prophetically maps out future international relations in East Asia. Roy Rogers & Gabby Hayes Signed Photo: A vintage 8x10 black-and-white publicity still showing both iconic Western screen stars in full costume, signed boldly across the image. Albert Schweitzer Aspen Visit (July 7, 1949): A striking portrait photograph of the philosopher and medical missionary, signed and dated during his historic summer visit to Aspen, Colorado. Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky Signed Cabinet Photo: An exceptional sepia vignette portrait photograph signed boldly across the image in Cyrillic script. The catalog hails this piece as perhaps the finest signed visual artifact of the legendary romantic composer in existence. Harriet Beecher Stowe Signed Quote: A crisp ink signature by the abolitionist author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, penning a biblical quote: "Trust in the Lord and do good." Booker T. Washington Tuskegee Appeal (January 27, 1894): A letter written on official school stationery to a New York judge. The iconic educator appeals for financial tuition sponsorships for poor but worthy Black students, written just one year prior to his historic "Atlanta Compromise" race-relations address. Mark Twain Faded Portrait (April 1909): A beautiful sepia-tone portrait showing the elderly humorist seated in a wooden chair, affectionately signed and inscribed: "Truly yours, Mark Twain. For Elizabeth."Elizabeth Taylor Nibbles and Me Hardcover (1946): A rare copy of the children's book written and illustrated entirely by a 13-year-old Elizabeth Taylor immediately following her breakout success in National Velvet. The book is warmly inscribed on the inside cover: "Lots of Love – From Nibbles & Elizabeth." Global Conflict & World War II Relics Erwin Rommel "Desert Fox" Postcard (September 9, 1939): A historic, mint-condition postcard handwritten in German by Rommel to his wife, Lucia Mollin, just eight days after the Nazi invasion of Poland sparked World War II. Rommel marvels at his new assignment commanding Hitler's guard battalion, writing with chilling confidence: "Things are going amazingly well for me... If we manage to maintain this pace, the war will be over in the West by the end of October, in my opinion." Admiral Chester Nimitz Propaganda handbill (February 1945): A wartime typed letter signed by Fleet Admiral Nimitz to an 1.1-year-old girl who shared his birthday. As a gift, Nimitz encloses an authentic U.S. propaganda bill dropped by Allied bombers over the Japanese mainland. The item is a 10-yen note printed on the back with a Japanese warning blasting the military cartel for wasting 5,000 yen per person on a losing war. Captured Okinawa "Rising Sun" Flag: An original silk Japanese military banner captured during the brutal Battle of Okinawa by a U.S. Army Major. The flag features printed margins translating to fierce nationalist slogans: "Our Military Strength Will Last Forever" and "Hoping for a Quick War." Gregory "Pappy" Boyington Flying Tigers Jacket: The authentic, black satin reversible flight jacket acquired directly from the estate of the legendary Marine Corps flying ace. The breast features embroidered stylized birds, the back showcases a fierce yellow tiger, and the reverse side maps out a detailed quilted green chart labeling major Japanese target cities around Mount Fuji. Charlie Owens D-Day Mapping Board (April 7, 1944): An original large perspective drawing accomplished in ink and pastel by the Los Angeles Times sketch artist. Dated exactly two months prior to the Allied invasion, the journalistic map utilizes sweeping arrows to project the exact troop movement paths that would be used on D-Day. Chaim Weizmann Palestine University Letter (July 10, 1903): A typed letter signed by the future first President of Israel, mapping out early zionist circulars to advocate for the foundation of a Jewish university in Palestine to combat academic discrimination in Europe.
